_comment: Shared hand surgery steps. Used by carpal tunnel release, trigger finger release and zone II flexor tendon repair.

step.hand.anaesthesia.title: Hand anaesthesia: wide-awake local or regional with tourniquet
step.hand.anaesthesia.why: The anaesthetic choice shapes the operation. Wide-awake local anaesthesia without tourniquet (WALANT) lets the patient move the finger during surgery, which shows whether a release is complete or a repair gaps, and avoids general anaesthesia and the arm tourniquet.
how: Agree the technique with the patient and the anaesthetist: WALANT, regional block with an arm tourniquet, or general anaesthesia.

For WALANT, inject local anaesthetic with adrenaline slowly through a fine needle, proximal to distal, and wait for vasoconstriction before incising; calculate the maximum safe dose by weight and record it.
Have the reversal agent for adrenaline vasoconstriction available per local protocol in case a digit stays pale.
Explain to the awake patient what they will feel and that you will ask them to move their fingers.
pitfalls: Incising before the adrenaline has had time to work, so the field bleeds.
Exceeding the weight-based maximum local anaesthetic dose in a bilateral or multiple-digit case.

step.hand.incision.title: Hand incision placed on the creases and safe lines
step.hand.incision.why: Incisions that cross flexion creases at a right angle contract and limit movement. Incisions planned on the creases, the mid-lateral line or as Brunner zigzags heal flat and can be extended safely.
how: Mark the incision before infiltration, relating it to the creases and to the structure you need to reach.
Use Brunner zigzags or mid-lateral incisions in the digit; never cross a flexion crease at a right angle.
Incise skin only, then spread in the subcutaneous fat in the line of the nerves before dividing any deeper tissue.
pitfalls: A straight longitudinal incision across a digital crease.
Cutting deeply in one pass in the palm or digit.

step.hand.nerve-protection.title: Identify and protect the nerves before dividing anything
step.hand.nerve-protection.why: In the hand the nerves lie close to every structure that is released or repaired, and their position varies. Seeing the nerve before cutting is the only reliable protection.
how: Know where the nerve is expected for this operation and look for it before dividing fascia, pulley or ligament.
Retract nerves gently with blunt retractors; never hold them with toothed forceps.
If a nerve is found divided or partially divided, record it and repair it under magnification with fine sutures, or arrange repair with the appropriate surgeon.
structuresAtRisk: Median nerve and its recurrent motor and palmar cutaneous branches
pitfalls: Assuming textbook anatomy when variants are common.
Dividing tissue that has not been seen on both sides.

step.hand.active-check.title: Active movement check before closure
step.hand.active-check.why: In a wide-awake patient, full active movement shows what no passive test can: whether triggering has gone, or whether a repair gaps or catches on a pulley. Correcting it now avoids a second operation.
how: Ask the patient to make a full fist and fully extend the digit several times.
Watch the tendon: it should glide smoothly without triggering, catching or gapping.
If movement is incomplete, find the cause (residual pulley, tight repair, bulky knot) and correct it, then repeat the check.
Under general or regional anaesthesia, use passive movement and the tenodesis effect, and record that an active check was not possible.
pitfalls: Testing only passive movement when the patient could have moved actively.

step.hand.unexpected-findings.title: Unexpected findings in the hand: stop and get help
step.hand.unexpected-findings.why: Hand operations booked as routine can reveal a tumour, a nerve variant, tenosynovitis, infection or a tendon gap that cannot be closed primarily. The wrong response is to improvise a reconstruction the patient did not consent to.
how: Stop and reassess the anatomy and the diagnosis before going further.
Send tissue for histology or culture if it looks abnormal.

If the planned operation cannot be completed safely (for example a tendon that cannot be repaired primarily), do the minimum safe procedure, close or cover, and plan a further operation with the patient's consent.
Call a senior hand surgeon when the finding is outside your experience, and record what was found and why the plan changed.
structuresAtRisk: Nerves and tendons in an unfamiliar anatomy
pitfalls: Extending the operation into a reconstruction without consent.
Discarding abnormal tissue without sending it.

step.hand.dressing-therapy.title: Hand dressing, elevation, splint and therapy plan
step.hand.dressing-therapy.why: Hand outcome depends on what happens after theatre: swelling and stiffness cause more poor results than technique does. The dressing, the position and the therapy plan are part of the operation.
how: Apply a dressing that does not constrict and leaves the fingertips visible for perfusion checks.
Splint in the position the operation needs, or leave the hand free to move if early motion is the plan.
Elevate the hand and start finger movement as instructed. Give written instructions on wound care, warning signs and suture removal.
Arrange hand therapy where the operation needs it, with the referral made before the patient leaves.
pitfalls: A circumferential dressing that tightens as the hand swells.
No therapy referral after a tendon repair.
